# Site selection for the first four stations

Before anything went in the ground, the group spent a weekend walking the lower half
of the valley to settle on four sites for the first stations. This records why those
four were picked over the alternatives that were walked and rejected on the same
trip.

## Access

Every site chosen had to be reachable on foot from a place a car could actually park,
carrying a rucksack of tools and no more, since nothing about this project involves
driving equipment up a track. A couple of otherwise decent spots higher up the valley
side were ruled out purely on this basis - fine ground, but a forty-minute walk each
way for a routine battery check was judged to be more than volunteers doing this at
weekends would keep up.

## Exposure

Each site needed a clear view of sky for the solar panel and reasonable exposure to
rainfall, which sounds obvious until you're actually stood in a valley full of trees
and hedgerows. One candidate site near the old mill was rejected for exactly this
reason: good access, good landowner relationship, but overhung by mature trees on
three sides, which would have starved the panel for a good part of the day and skewed
the rain readings under the canopy besides.

## Landowner permission

All four chosen sites sit on land where a personal connection to the landowner made
asking straightforward, which mattered more than it probably should have to how
quickly this got off the ground. Two further candidate sites looked good on paper but
the group either couldn't identify who owned the land or didn't have any existing
relationship to open the conversation with, and rather than cold-calling strangers
about bolting equipment to their field, those sites were shelved rather than pursued.

## Distance from the collector

The four sites were also chosen to sit within a radio hop or two of the collector at
the valley bottom, since with no network infrastructure of its own yet the group
wanted the first stations to prove the radio link worked before pushing further up
the valley where hops would need to relay through intermediate sites that didn't
exist. This kept the geographic spread of the first four fairly tight compared with
where the network has ended up since.

## What this doesn't cover

This is about where the stations physically sit, not about the radio band or hardware
used to get their readings back - that decision came later and is recorded
separately. Anyone looking for the reasoning on LoRa versus the alternatives
considered should look there instead; this document is about ground, fences, and who
owns them.
